page_title: Things they didn't teach you about Software Engineering

sources.entry: Things they didn't teach you about Software Engineering

summary.title: Things they didn't teach you about Software Engineering
summary.one_liner: A practitioner's list of real-world software engineering lessons that university rarely covers, such as working on legacy code, the importance of domain knowledge and documentation, and dealing with uncertainty and estimates.
keywords: dealing with uncertainty in software projects
takeaways: Most professional work is maintaining and refactoring large existing codebases rather than writing from scratch.
Domain knowledge and debugging/engineering fundamentals both matter; neither alone is enough.
Documentation, failsafes (circuit breakers, retries, fallbacks) and writing things down help survive other people's mess and incidents.
Treat every layer (own code, libraries, OS, hardware) as potentially buggy and design for failure.
Expect uncertainty, estimation requests, and meetings; the author suggests coarse estimates refined over time and insisting on agendas.
summary.summary: The author, a long-time software engineer, shares a subjective list of lessons from industry work that were missing from their education. Topics include mostly maintaining legacy code, the role of domain knowledge versus coding skill, the neglect of documentation and debugging, focusing on business value, working around poor vendors or managers, handling vague requirements, assuming bugs at every layer, the downsides of the job, estimation, and meetings. The piece is an informal essay rather than a technical tutorial, with brief anecdotes and no code. The page also contains many reader comments that mostly agree, with some disagreeing about work-life balance and whether aesthetics can be taught.
